speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Fake news is a global phenomenon and it can result in serious consequences for individuals and society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Fake news can be circulated easily, speedily, widely on social media.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Therefore, the circulation of fake news has to be taken seriously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a problem that needs to be dealt with quickly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To put it in perspective, we are not talking about trivial factual inaccuracies, but falsehoods that can cause real harm.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look internationally, one fake news story last year claimed that Mrs Hillary Clinton was running a paedophilia ring operating out of a pizza restaurant.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One man turned up with an assault rifle and opened fire in the restaurant.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Commentators have generally concluded that fake news can also be used as a powerful tool to interfere in domestic politics and domestic affairs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, before the United States (US) presidential elections, there were several fake news stories, huge numbers, claiming that Mrs Clinton sold weapons to the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria (ISIS).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Before the "Brexit" referendum, misleading stories were published to fuel xenophobia and anti-immigrant sentiment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: News articles published by foreign-controlled websites were said to be skewed and intended to influence a crucial referendum in Italy last year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are not isolated incidents and countries are beginning to grapple with them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Media reports have suggested that there were serious attempts to influence the US presidential elections, and perhaps they indeed were influenced, such as the "Brexit" referendum, the referendum in Italy, and there are attempts to influence the upcoming elections in Germany and France as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, there are suggestions that many of the fake news stories during the US elections were created by teenagers from a small town in Macedonia.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They had no interest in the US elections.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of course, countries may well be involved as well, organised to attack and destabilise other countries during elections, and at other times.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The whole idea is to spread sensational news, sensational headlines, influence the population, and arrive at the outcome that is wanted by a certain country outside.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Often also it makes money, because the more people access their fake news, the more advertising revenue the originators earn.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is really easy money for the fake news factories.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Many countries have called for a tough stance to be taken against fake news, including the US, the United Kingdom (UK) and Germany, or to put in place more effective measures to counter fake news.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Germany, for example, is considering a draft law that will require social networks, websites, including Facebook, to remove fake news which amounts to illegal content from their platforms.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Social networks which fail to comply with such a request could face very stiff fines.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The UK has also been reported to have launched a parliamentary probe into fake news, calling it a threat to democracy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Fake news has been a problem in Singapore, not quite at the level that I have listed in other countries, but we see the phenomenon.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has not had that much of an impact yet, but you can predict that the same sequence of actors, foreign countries, foreign agencies, people sitting outside of Singapore using it to either destabilise our society or not caring whether it destabilises but doing it to make a lot of money.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One example of a site that regularly purveyed fake news was, of course, "The Real Singapore".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is impossible to list all the fake news they published but I can give some examples.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2015, Thaipusam, it claimed that there was a commotion between the Police and participants, and that this was sparked off by a complaint by a Filipino family.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One of the editors altered an article from a reader and then inserted falsehoods into the article and passed it off as facts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Yang Kaiheng, one of the owners who went to jail, boasted about earning $4,000 to $5,000 a month.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Last August, it claimed that there was near-zero turnout for the late former President SR Nathan's funeral, and that kindergarten children were forced to attend.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was an attempt to paint him as an unpopular President.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said, it has not reached the levels of what is happening elsewhere, but this is an example.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is a table that we have prepared which sets out some of the falsehoods from the "States Times Review" and my Ministry will load that together with my answer to the Parliamentary Question on our website.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even when the articles are not totally fake, they are highly misleading, and the whole purpose is to purvey falsehoods and mislead the public.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have incidents of online hoaxes going viral in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The headline was accompanied by a completely unrelated photograph of an innocent Singaporean, Mr Prakash Hetamsaria.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Hetamsaria was subjected to online abuse and xenophobic racist comments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Police and Singapore Civil Defence Force had to be mobilised and deployed to investigate the claim.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Taxpayers pay the cost for all of this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Another anonymous post widely circulated on social media falsely claimed that a childcare centre at River Valley Road made their children sleep on the floor and eat rotten fruits, suggesting child neglect.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of course, there was a public outcry, but you can imagine the impact on the childcare operator.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Hoaxes like these, articles like these, can have real-world consequences, if not quickly corrected.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They can cause harm to Singaporeans, alarm to the public, emergency resources will have to be diverted, and the reputation of businesses and people can be completely, unreasonably, unfairly damaged.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All because some nasty people seek to profit from this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said, there is a much more serious dimension to all of this because fake news today, we must assume, can be used as an offensive weapon by foreign agencies and foreign countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have already seen examples of that − to get into your public's mind, to destabilise your public, to psychologically weaken them and impact your agencies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is a very serious threat and it will be naive for us to believe that governments or state agencies do not engage in this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Under our current law, there are limited remedies to deal with these falsehoods.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, it is an offence under the Telecommunications Act to transmit a message knowing that it is false.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But these remedies are ineffective; they were really looking at a time before the new age as it were.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The circulation of falsehoods can go viral very quickly today.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will announce our position once we have completed our review.
